title: How to Measure a Part for Printing
description: Bring or send a photo of the broken part along with its dimensions. Use a ruler or calipers for accuracy — even rough measurements help us get started.
content:
Before ordering a 3D print of a part, accurate measurements make all the difference. The more precisely you can describe the part, the faster we can model and print it, and the closer the final result will be to what you expected.

Start with a photo. Place the part on a flat surface next to a ruler or a familiar object (a coin, a charger) for scale. Make sure the photo is well-lit and taken straight on, not at an angle, so proportions stay true.

Then measure the key dimensions with a ruler or calipers: length, width, height, and the diameter of any holes or shafts. Note the thickness of walls and any grooves, tabs, or slots that need to match exactly.

If the part is broken and you only have fragments, do not worry. We can work from a photo of the remaining pieces and your measurements. Even rough numbers help us get started and produce a working prototype quickly.

title: PLA vs PETG: Which Material to Choose
description: PLA is great for decorative items and prototypes. PETG is stronger and more heat-resistant — better for parts that will be used outdoors or under stress.
content:
Choosing the right material can determine whether your printed part lasts a week or a decade. The two most common options in our workshop are PLA and PETG, and each has its place.

PLA is the go-to for decorative items, prototypes, and anything that stays indoors. It is easy to print, available in a wide range of colours and finishes, and very affordable. Its main weakness is heat: PLA softens around 60°C, so it is a poor choice for parts that sit near engines, radiators, or in direct summer sun.

PETG is stronger, tougher, and handles heat and impact much better. It withstands outdoor weather, resists most chemicals, and is a favourite for functional parts such as brackets, mounts, and protective covers. It costs a little more and takes a bit longer to print, but for parts that will actually be used, it is usually worth it.

If you are unsure which material fits your part, tell us how and where you plan to use it. We will point you to the right option and explain exactly what to expect from each.

title: Why Local Printing Beats Online Orders
description: No shipping wait, no minimum order. Walk in, describe what you need, and get it printed the same day in most cases.
content:
Ordering a spare part online usually means long shipping delays, high delivery costs, and minimum order requirements. Printing locally in Suntar removes all three obstacles.

No shipping wait. Once we confirm your model, most parts are ready within a day. Instead of waiting weeks for a package to cross the country, you pick up your part in person or receive it via local delivery.

No minimum order. Many online services require a minimum spend or batch size. With us, a single small part is just as welcome as a full set. You pay for what you need, nothing more.

Direct communication. You can bring in the broken part, describe the problem in your own words, and ask questions while we work. If something needs adjusting, we fix it on the spot and you see the result immediately.

For most projects, local printing is simply faster, cheaper, and much more flexible than ordering from the other side of the globe.

title: From Sketch to Finished Part in One Day
description: A short tour of how a simple request becomes a printed part: design, slicing, printing, and post-processing — often finished the same day.
content:
Have you ever wondered how a 3D print goes from an idea to a finished object? Here is what happens inside our workshop after you make a request.

Design. If your part needs to be modeled from scratch, the first step is creating a 3D model. We work from photos, measurements, or a reference object to build a model that matches your part as closely as possible.

Slicing. Once the model is ready, we import it into slicing software. This step decides how the part will be printed, layer by layer: orientation on the printer bed, density of the infill, and the thickness of each layer all affect strength, speed, and surface quality.

Printing. The printer builds the part by melting plastic filament and laying it down in thin layers. Simple parts can take a couple of hours; larger or more detailed ones may take most of the day.

Post-processing. After printing we remove supports, sand the surface where needed, and do the final check. The result is a clean, finished part ready for you to pick up.

Most single-part orders fit comfortably into one working day. Drop by in the morning and collect your part by the evening.

title: ABS, TPU and Beyond: Special Filaments
description: Beyond PLA and PETG we also print with ABS and flexible TPU. Learn when these materials make sense for your project.
content:
While PLA and PETG cover most orders, some parts simply cannot do without a more specialized material. Here is an overview of what we keep on the shelves.

ABS is the classic choice for automotive and appliance parts. It is impact-resistant and tolerates higher temperatures than PLA. One thing to keep in mind is that ABS tends to shrink while cooling, so large flat parts may need a heated enclosure, which we have.

TPU is a flexible filament used for gaskets, phone cases, bumpers, and anything that needs to bend. Depending on the grade, the printed part can be soft like a rubber band or firm like a bicycle tire. Printing TPU is slower, but the flexibility it adds cannot be replicated by rigid plastics.

Nylon is an option for heavy-duty mechanical parts that face constant wear and abrasion. It is strong, durable, and tough to break, which makes it a favourite for gears and bushings.

If you are not sure what material your part needs, bring it in and describe how you will use it. We will suggest the right filament and, if needed, print a quick test piece before making the full part.

title: How to Make Your Parts Last Longer
description: Service life depends a lot on design. A few simple tips on walls, fillets, and infill that help printed parts survive real use.
content:
A well-designed part can outlast the original it replaces. Strength in 3D printing comes from more than just the material — it comes from the way the part is shaped and printed.

Give walls enough thickness. A part with thin walls flexes and breaks easily. Adding just a few extra millimetres of wall thickness dramatically increases strength for a small increase in print time.

Round the corners. Sharp internal corners concentrate stress and become natural cracking points. Fillets (rounded corners) spread that stress and make the part far more durable under real loads.

Choose the right infill. Lighter infill saves time and material, but for load-bearing parts a denser infill keeps the part stiff. As a rule of thumb: decorative items around 15%, functional parts 40%, and parts under heavy load up to 80%.

Print orientation matters. Parts are weaker between layers than along them. Whenever possible we rotate the model so the most stressed direction is printed along the layer lines, not across them.

Tell us what the part will be used for and we will build those protections into the model from the start.
